title: Psychology on Trial
lead: Ten classic psychology experiments, ten minutes a day. Every morning your professor Dr Hale opens one case. You take part in it, read the objections, and decide what is left of the result.
how: Every day you open one case with Dr Hale, your professor. A day takes about ten minutes.
Some choices are your own opinion, with no right or wrong. Some check your reading, and some check how carefully you write. A red ✕ shows a slip and a better sentence.
Tap an underlined word to see what it means. Open "Sources" at the end of each day to see where the facts come from.

decisions.q: What do you say to the experimenter?
good: I'm not comfortable going on. I would like to stop now.
I'm sorry, but I won't continue unless someone checks on him.
wrong: Stop this at once! You are a monster!

Give in: "All right. I will go on."

decisions.q: Which version is the most careful and accurate?
good: The results suggest that many ordinary people may keep following instructions even when this causes serious distress to someone else.
In this set-up, most volunteers were willing to continue to the end, which suggests that a situation can be more powerful than people expect.
wrong: The study proves that everybody is a potential torturer.
The results suggest that many people tends to obey authority.

decisions.q: What did Haslam, Reicher and Birney find in their analogue study?
good: Appeals to the value of science were more effective than orders.
wrong: Orders worked better than any other prod.

decisions.q: Which version reports the criticism most carefully?
good: Some researchers argue that the volunteers were responding to appeals to science rather than to orders.
Archival evidence suggests that doubt about the set-up may have influenced how far some volunteers went.
wrong: The critics have proved that Milgram made up his results.
According to Perry, many volunteers doubts the shocks were real.

decisions.q: What do the variations in Milgram's study suggest?
good: That the situation strongly affects how far people go, and that support from others makes refusal much easier.
wrong: That obedience does not depend on the situation.
That the lab coat was the only thing that mattered.
That Milgram's first result was a mistake.

Claim: "Situations can push many people further than they expect." What is its status?
